title.en: Baqahol Buys a Kingship and the Jaguars Tear It Down
title.zh: 巴克霍爾以寶石購王位，豹獸拆毀之

region.en: Pantzic and Paraxone (dawn stations of the Cakchiquel), Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 潘茲與帕拉雄（卡克奇克爾的黎明之地），危地馬拉高地

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 39-40

summary.en: At the first settlement — the tribe's 'day-breaking' — Baqahol arrives last and claims the kingship: 'I am king, I received you.' Refused, he offers a carved precious stone, is refused again, builds himself a stronghold, and has his works demolished by the Chuluc Balam beasts sent by Gagavitz, who resents the usurpation.
summary.zh: 在初次定居——族人的「黎明之時」——巴克霍爾最後抵達，卻宣稱王位：「我是王，我接納了你們。」遭拒後，他獻上一方雕琢寶石，再遭拒；遂自建要塞，但其工事被加加維茨所遣的「楚盧克豹」獸拆除——加加維茨不容其竊據。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: The first who went forth were Gekaquch, Baqahol, Cibakihay and Cavek, who came together — you were the first, oh my tribe, to bring about our day-breaking, some time before the dawn. There their dawn appeared, there they built houses, and there took place the marriage of their chief named Nimahay.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 39; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The last who arrived was Baqahol, and they had already begun to build when he came. He said to Gekaquch: 'I, I am king, I received you.' The others answered: 'Thou! no, thou art not our king; we do not wish you to be our king.' Then he showed them a precious stone and said: 'I will give you this precious stone carved with four feet, and hands and toes, if I am your chief.' But that suited them not.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 39; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then he began to build himself a stronghold, and soon the labor was completed, for he coveted the power. For this reason his constructions were destroyed by the Chuluc Balam sent by Gagavitz, because Gagavitz liked it not that Baqahol desired the leadership. After that the day-breaking took place on Pantzic and Paraxone, each clothed with changing green.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 39-40; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Bathing and Anointing of a Chief

region.zh: 伊辛切地區，危地馬拉高地

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, sec. 41

summary.en: The Annals preserve the ceremony by which a chief entered power: bathed by attendants in a large painted vessel, clad in flowing robes, girded with the sacred fillet, anointed with the holy colors, and adorned with jewels — the moment when a household head becomes a ruling chief.
summary.zh: 《紀年》保存了酋長就任之儀：由侍者在大彩盆中為其沐浴，披流衣，繫聖帶，以聖色塗身，佩以寶石——家戶之首由此成為執政酋長。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Then the chief entered upon his royalty: he was seated on the seat of power, and then he was bathed in the bathing-vessel with its yellow water and its flowers. He was bathed by the attendants in a large painted vessel; he was clad in flowing robes; a sacred girdle or fillet was tied upon him; he was painted with the holy colors, was anointed, and jewels were placed upon his person.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 41; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Thus the chief of the clan was raised above his house, and all the warriors in the settlement were arrayed by their houses and clans in the same order. The whole people were numbered within the settlement, and the royalty was shared and judged by the households, so that power was measured, counted, and distributed like the days themselves.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 41; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Cay Noh and Cay Batz Hide in the Cave Within a Cave
title.zh: 卡伊·諾與卡伊·巴茲匿於洞中之洞

region.zh: 佩克帕魯佩克洞穴，危地馬拉高地

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 51-55

summary.en: Sons of Gagavitz, the two brothers shine like fire by night and shake the earth like Cabrakan as they collect Tepeuh's tribute. Betrothed by the Ahtziquinahay's daughters who steal their treasure jar, they marry the chief's daughters and dare not face the king who sent them: they hide in Pecparupec, the cave within a cave, until Tepeuh's forgiveness brings them out to rule.
summary.zh: 加加維茨之子兄弟二人，夜行如火炬，行地如卡布拉坎撼地震動，代特佩烏收取貢賦。阿希基納哈伊之女偷走其寶罐，兄弟因而聯姻酋長之女，卻不敢面對遣其前來之王：遂匿於佩克帕魯佩克——洞中之洞——直至特佩烏赦免，方出而執政。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Our ancestors Caynoh and Caybatz came to Tepeuh. 'Who are you?' was said to them. 'We are the sons of Gagavitz,' they replied, and Tepeuh marveled greatly, and strengthened them, for they were humble before him. They were then sent to collect the tribute from the tribes, and no one of the many people died while they were taking it.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 51; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Truly all feared their magic power and wisdom: where they were at night it shone like fire, and there was trembling as of an earthquake. Quite to the far East they were paid what they demanded, precious metals and spun stuffs, by the tribes from whom they took tribute. Mighty were their words.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 52; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: They came to collect tribute from the Ahtziquinahay, and the Ahtziquinahay said among themselves: 'Let us make these messengers of Tepeuh our sons-in-law; we will give them women and take back what they have designated.' Indeed the daughters of the chiefs came secretly and stole the jar of treasures while the brothers slept, and Caynoh and Caybatz took them as wives.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 53; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then our ancestors, not seeing their treasure, were filled with fear: 'You have indeed ruined us, oh you Ahtziquinahay! Tepeuh will be angered against us.' They went to speak with Tepeuh, but did not reach him, for they feared to come before him; so they hid themselves in a cavern and retired into the cavern. The place where they hid was called by Caynoh Pecparupec — a cave within a cave — and the tribe sought them there until Tepeuh forgave them and they came out to rule.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 53-55; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: King Qikab Humbled by His Own Sons

region.zh: 古馬卡（烏塔特蘭），基切王都，危地馬拉

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 79-82

summary.en: The Quiche revolt against their own king Qikab: his sons Tatayac and Ah Itza side with the people, refuse him tribute, and kill his chiefs of the royal service. Twice the old king humbles himself before the populace, giving up his jewels, his metals, and finally the royal power itself — 'since then the people acted, and the king is made such by the people.'
summary.zh: 基切人反叛其王基卡布：其子塔塔雅克與阿伊察站於民眾一邊，拒納貢賦，誅殺王室之臣。老王兩度向民眾俯首，交出寶石、金屬，終至交出王權本身——「自此而後，民眾行事，王由民眾所立」。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Then began a revolt against the king Qikab by the Quiche men; the family of the king was the cause of the contest. The Quiches would not promise the homage as vassals which he asked of them; they wished that the roads should be free to the Quiche people, which the king would not grant.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 79; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Tatayac and Ah Itza, the two distinguished sons of the king, took the part of the Quiches, and the king was thus opposed to his own sons, who incited the people not to pay their dues; for they coveted the royal power, and desired the precious stones, the metals, the slaves and people of their father. A council of the Quiches was held against the warriors maintained by the king, and they began to put to death all those of the first rank in the royal service.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 80; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The king Qikab humbled himself before the people, trying to appease them with his precious stones and metals; he gave up the power of the rulers to the people and divided with them his royal rights. The heart of the king was bruised by his sons, by that which they had done. Then perished the ancient glory of the nation: since then the people acted, and the king is made such by the people.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 81; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Iximche on the Ratzamut Is Founded
title.zh: 伊辛切建城於拉察姆特

region.zh: 伊辛切（特克潘危地馬拉），奇馬爾特南戈，危地馬拉

texts.period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604 (city founded c. 1470s); Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 82-85

summary.en: After another revolt, the four rulers — Huntoh, Vukubatz, Chuluc, and Xitamal Queh — quit Chiavar, burn the roads twice behind them, and establish Iximche on the Ratzamut, the almost inaccessible plain ringed by ravines. The warriors of the seven nations rejoice: 'You have done well to come here to Iximche' — and the glory of the Quiches disappears.
summary.zh: 另一次反叛之後，四王——洪托、武庫巴茲、楚盧克與希塔馬爾·克——離開奇亞瓦爾，兩度焚路於身後，建城伊辛切於拉察姆特——四周環以深谷、幾不可達的平地。七族戰士皆喜：「你們來到伊辛切，做得很好」——基切的榮光從此消逝。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Then another revolt began against the four leaders, Huntoh, Vukubatz, Chuluc and Xitamal Queh, occasioned by a woman of the Zotzils Tukuches; and after twice burning the roads behind them, they established the town of Iximche on the Ratzamut and settled there, the four rulers, the sovereigns of the Cakchiquel people.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 82; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: As soon as they were settled, they placed themselves in readiness for war with the Quiches, and our ancestors built a stronghold. All the people rejoiced at the establishment of the city by these illustrious heroes; for they had fought on the side of the king Qikab, and therefore all the warriors of the seven nations rejoiced.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 83; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The warriors of the seven nations gave their words when the city of Iximche was founded: 'You have done well to leave Chiavar, my brother; you have done well to come here to Iximche. There was but one brave man with Cavek and the Quiches; but hereafter he will not go to war with the Quiches.' And when war came, two strongholds of the Quiches were seized, Qizqab was killed at Xechituh, and thus disappeared the glory of the Quiches.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 83-85; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Four Heroines of the Eleventh Ah
title.zh: 十一阿赫之日的四位女傑

region.zh: 伊辛切，奇馬爾特南戈，危地馬拉

texts.period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604 (revolt of 1496); Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 101-103

summary.en: On the day 11 Ah the great insurrection breaks out at Iximche: the Tukuches are drawn out of the city and slaughtered at the bridgehead. Four women arm themselves with lances and bows, fight as four young men, and their arrows strike the very mat of the enemy captain Chucuybatzin; images of these heroines are later set up before the Zotzil and Xahil buildings.
summary.zh: 十一阿赫之日，伊辛切大暴動爆發：楚庫切人被逐出城，於橋頭遭屠戮。四位女子持矛張弓而戰，勇如四名少年，其箭直中敵將楚庫伊巴欽的坐席；此後，這些女傑的塑像被立於佐茲爾與薩希爾建築之前。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: The day of the revolt was appointed by the chief Cay Hunahpu, and on this day, 11th Ah, the revolt broke out. The Tukuches were drawn out of the city to the other side of the river, and all their warriors went there also, that they might enter the city; but the warriors of the kings Cablahuh Tihax and Oxlahuh tzy opposed them.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 101; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: When the dawn appeared on the day 11th Ah, the Tukuches began on the opposite side from the city, and the drums and trumpets of the chief Cay Hunahpu were heard. Then the warriors armed and displayed their brilliant feathers, shining banners, gold and precious stones. Truly it was terrible for the number of the Tukuches, who could not be counted by eight thousands nor by sixteen thousands.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 102; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: There were four women who had armed themselves with lances and bows and taken part in the battle, fully equal to four young men. The arrows launched by these heroines struck the very mat of Chucuybatzin. The chiefs of the battle afterwards set up the images of these women before the buildings of the Zotzils and the Xahils, whence these women had gone forth.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 102; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then began a general attack on the Tukuches; they were cut to pieces at once; no one resisted; the rout was complete; men, women and children were given up to slaughter. The chief Cay Hunahpu was slain, and those of Tibaqoy and Raxakan retired, partly to Quiche, partly among the Tzutuhils, and were thus dispersed. Such was the destruction of the Tukuches, in old times, oh my children.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 103; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Tunatiuh Comes to Iximche and Burns the K'iche' Kings
title.zh: 圖納提烏至伊辛切，焚基切諸王

region.zh: 伊辛切，奇馬爾特南戈，危地馬拉

texts.period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604 (events of 1524); Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 144-149

summary.en: The Castilians arrive at Xetulul; Tunatiuh (Alvarado) destroys the Quiche nation before Xelahuh, burns three K'iche' chiefs alive, and demands Cakchiquel warriors for the slaughter. He enters Iximche without a fight, is feasted, and asks with terrible courtesy for more warriors: 'I want to make war with them.'
summary.zh: 卡斯蒂利亞人抵達希圖盧爾；圖納提烏（阿爾瓦拉多）在希拉胡之前摧毀基切族，將基切三王活活燒死，並索要卡克奇克爾戰士以行殺戮。他不戰而入伊辛切，受宴之後，以可怕而客氣的口吻再索戰士：「我要與他們作戰。」

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: It was during this year that the Castilians arrived. Forty-nine years have passed since the Castilians came to Xepit and Xetulul. On the day 1 Ganel the Quiches were destroyed by the Castilians. Tunatiuh Avilantaro, as he was called, conquered all the towns. Their countenances were previously unknown, and the people rendered homage to sticks and stones.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 144; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: On their arrival at Xelahuh, the Quiche nation was routed and destroyed; all of them had hastened there to oppose the Castilians, and there the Quiche nation was destroyed in front of Xelahuh. He then went to the city Gumarcaah, and there came before him the chiefs, the king and the next in rank, and tribute was paid by the Quiches; and the chiefs suffered many torments from Tunatiuh.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 145-146; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: On the day 4 Qat three chiefs, the king and the next in rank, were burned alive by Tunatiuh, nor was the heart of Tunatiuh satisfied with war. Soon a messenger from Tunatiuh came to the chiefs: 'Let the warriors of the Ahpozotzils and Ahpoxahils come to the slaughter of the Quiches! I want to make war with them.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 147-148; not verbatim throughout.
